questions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the three pillars of COA audit?

options.text: Regularity
Legality
Economy
Aesthetics

rationale.a: Regularity is the first pillar—verifying procedures were followed.
rationale.b: Legality is the second pillar—verifying code and law compliance.
rationale.c: Economy is the third pillar—verifying cost control and resource efficiency.
rationale.d: Aesthetics, while important to architects, is not a statutory COA audit criterion.
rationale.correct: COA audits examine accounts for revenue/expenditures and promulgate rules against irregular, unnecessary, excessive, extravagant, or unconscionable uses of funds. Aesthetics is not an audit criterion.
rationale.takeaway: COA's three audit pillars are regularity, legality, and economy—aesthetics is not a COA audit measure.

questions.text: What does 'regularity' mean in the context of COA audit?

options.text: The building is constructed on time, which is a scheduling concern rather than a compliance issue
Established procedures were followed, bidding was conducted per RA 9184, and authorizations were documented
The design is aesthetically pleasing, which is subjective and not a compliance measure
The project costs less than budgeted, which is a financial outcome rather than a procedural compliance

rationale.a: Schedule compliance is not the definition of regularity in audit context.
rationale.c: Aesthetics is not a regularity measure; regularity concerns procedural compliance.
rationale.d: Cost savings, while related to economy, do not define regularity; following procedures defines it.
rationale.correct: Regularity means established procedures were followed: RA 9184 procurement, proper approvals obtained, authorizations documented—creating an audit trail of compliance.
rationale.takeaway: Regularity in COA audit means established procedures were followed, proper approvals documented, and RA 9184 procurement conducted.

questions.text: Why is professional liability insurance important for architects working on publicly funded projects, and what does it typically cover?

options.text: It is optional and covers all misconduct, including minor infractions
It protects both architect and client if design errors cause problems; typically covers negligent acts, errors, and omissions but not willful misconduct or fraud
It only covers attorney fees, excluding other legal costs
It covers aesthetic disagreements, providing a basis for resolving design disputes

rationale.a: Insurance is standard practice (often required); it does not cover intentional wrongdoing.
rationale.c: Liability insurance covers design error costs; attorney fees may be included but are not the primary coverage.
rationale.d: Aesthetic disagreements are not design errors; liability covers negligent acts, not aesthetic preferences.
rationale.correct: Professional liability insurance is essential for public projects; it covers negligent acts and errors but excludes willful misconduct and fraud (which are uninsurable).
rationale.takeaway: Professional liability insurance covers negligent design errors and omissions but excludes willful misconduct and fraud.

questions.text: What does COA typically scrutinize when a project experiences frequent or costly change orders?

options.text: Only the contractor's performance and adherence to the original contract specifications and timeline
Whether the preliminary design phase was thorough and whether design scope was adequately defined
The architect's personal preferences and design choices that do not directly affect the project budget or scope
Only the project location and the environmental clearance issued by the local government unit

rationale.a: While contractor performance matters, COA focuses on design completeness that could have prevented changes.
rationale.c: Architect preferences are irrelevant; the issue is whether design and scope were sufficiently defined.
rationale.d: Project location is irrelevant to change order scrutiny.
rationale.correct: Frequent changes signal inadequate preliminary design or poor scope definition; COA investigates whether the design phase was sufficiently thorough.
rationale.takeaway: Frequent change orders prompt COA scrutiny of preliminary design thoroughness and scope adequacy.

questions.text: What is the first document architects should prepare to demonstrate design compliance for COA review?

options.text: fee proposal, including a detailed breakdown of costs and services
preliminary studies and feasibility report showing design rationale
marketing brochure with visualizations and client testimonials
An insurance certificate covering potential design liabilities

rationale.a: Fee proposals are financial documents unrelated to design justification or compliance.
rationale.c: Marketing brochures lack the technical depth required to explain design decisions.
rationale.d: Insurance certificates prove financial capacity but not design compliance.
rationale.correct: Preliminary studies and feasibility reports establish design rationale, demonstrating that design decisions were based on systematic analysis and justification.
rationale.takeaway: Preliminary studies and feasibility reports are the foundation for defending design decisions to COA auditors.

questions.text: What key information must every change order include?

options.text: Only the cost increase, without any reference to schedule or scope changes
Description of change, reason, scope impact, fee/schedule impact, and signatures of architect and client
Only the schedule impact, ignoring any cost or scope alterations
Only the client name, excluding any details about the change itself

rationale.a: Cost alone is incomplete; reason and scope documentation are essential for audit.
rationale.c: Schedule impact alone is incomplete; description, reason, and cost must also be documented.
rationale.d: Client name is basic identification; substantive change documentation is required.
rationale.correct: Change orders must comprehensively document: what changed, why it was necessary, what additional work results, and impacts on fee and schedule—with signatures for authorization.
rationale.takeaway: Change orders must document change description, reason, scope impact, fee/schedule impacts, and authorized signatures.

questions.text: How should an architect document compliance with technical standards such as NBC and BP 344 for COA review?

options.text: Verbal assurance is sufficient, provided it is given by a senior architect with relevant experience
Code compliance checklist, consultant memos on adequacy, and evidence of building official approval before bidding
Only final photographs, as they provide visual proof of compliance with the standards
No documentation is required, as compliance is assumed based on professional integrity

rationale.a: Verbal claims lack documentary evidence required for audit verification.
rationale.c: Photographs document as-built conditions but not design-phase compliance verification.
rationale.d: COA audits require systematic compliance documentation; none is unacceptable.
rationale.correct: Documentation includes: code compliance checklist signed by architect, structural/MEP consultant memos confirming adequacy, and building official approval evidence before construction.
rationale.takeaway: Code compliance documentation requires checklist, consultant memos, and building official approval—all completed before construction begins.

questions.text: What must an architect maintain to prove proper procurement compliance under RA 9184 in case of COA audit?

options.text: Only the final invoice, which must be detailed and itemized according to project specifications
BAC minutes, qualifications evaluation, contract award decision, and signed service agreement
Only verbal agreements, which are documented through meeting notes and confirmed via email correspondence
No documentation needed, as compliance is assumed through project completion and client satisfaction

rationale.a: Final invoice alone does not demonstrate procurement procedure compliance.
rationale.c: Verbal agreements lack documentary evidence; written, signed agreements are mandatory.
rationale.d: Complete procurement documentation is required for COA audit verification.
rationale.correct: Procurement compliance documentation includes BAC meeting minutes, qualifications evaluation results, award decision, and signed service agreement establishing scope and authority.
rationale.takeaway: Procurement compliance documentation requires BAC minutes, qualifications evaluation, award decision, and signed service agreement.

questions.text: What is the appropriate response strategy if an architect receives a valid COA audit finding regarding design performance?

options.text: Ignore the finding and continue past practices, assuming no changes are necessary
Become defensive and refuse to respond, believing the audit to be unjustified
Acknowledge the finding, explain the circumstances, and describe corrective actions for future projects
Blame the contractor for not following the design, deflecting responsibility

rationale.a: Ignoring findings demonstrates unprofessionalism and prevents improvement.
rationale.b: Defensive, evasive responses harm credibility and suggest guilt.
rationale.d: Blaming others without acknowledging architect's role damages professional relationships and credibility.
rationale.correct: Professional response to valid findings acknowledges the issue, explains context, and demonstrates commitment to improvement through corrective actions.
rationale.takeaway: Valid COA findings should be acknowledged, explained, and addressed with concrete corrective actions for future projects.

questions.text: What is the primary role of the Commission on Audit (COA) in government-funded projects?

options.text: To provide design advice, ensuring that all architectural plans meet the necessary aesthetic and functional standards
To conduct financial and performance audits ensuring regularity, legality, and economy
To hire architects, selecting those with the best qualifications for government projects
To approve architectural designs, verifying compliance with all relevant building codes and regulations

rationale.a: COA reviews outcomes, not design strategy; design advice is not COA's role.
rationale.c: COA does not hire personnel; it audits spending and compliance.
rationale.d: Building officials approve designs; COA audits compliance after fact.
rationale.correct: COA conducts financial and performance audits evaluating regularity (procedures followed), legality (code compliance), and economy (cost control).
rationale.takeaway: COA audits government projects for regularity, legality, and economy—encompassing design decisions and cost control.

questions.code_citation: 1987 Constitution Art. IX-D; COA Auditing Rules
